intro: You are looking at the Library of Celsus at Ephesus, built between the AD 110s and 135. Take in this marble front, but know that it is more than a library's face: it is also the face of a tomb, for Celsus' sarcophagus still lies in the chamber beneath the apse. The model shows the façade re-erected in 1970-78 at its full height, and the hall behind it only as high as its walls survive.
spot-1: Now you are looking at the statue of Sophia. She stands for Wisdom, one of the four virtues on the front. Enjoy her here in the model, because the original now lives far away, in Vienna.
spot-2: Now you are looking at the central doorway, the widest of the three doors. Imagine stepping through it: beyond the porch behind it lay the reading room.
spot-3: Now look up to the upper-storey window. This is where the light came in to fill the hall, while along the walls inside, the shelves stood in their niches.
spot-4: Now you are looking at a segmental pediment. Notice how the three pediments alternate: triangular in the middle, segmental on either side.
spot-5: Now you are looking at the nine steps. Running the full width of the building, they climb from the courtyard up to the front.
spot-6: Now you are looking at the apse, the semicircular niche at the back of the hall. Beneath it lies Celsus' sarcophagus, resting here still.
uncertainty: Finally, let us be honest about what this model does not know. The width and height of the façade are measured. The rhythm of the front, with four pairs of columns, three doorways between them, three windows above and the triangular and segmental pediments over those, is read from photographs of the front re-erected in 1970-78. How the two orders divide the 16 metres, the column diameters and the poses of the statues are a matter of proportion rather than measurement. The four virtues in the niches and the two male figures above are modelled down to the folds of their dress, yet they are not copies of the originals in Vienna: their poses and clothing are interpretation. The bronze statues on the two bases by the stair are lost; they stand in scans of two real Roman togate statues of the period, the Arringatore and the veiled Tiberius. The acanthus and volutes of the capitals are modelled, but they do not copy the carving on the stone, the inscriptions on the architraves and bases carry their real Greek and Latin texts, though their line breaks and letter sizes are the model's, and the Ennoia base is lettered on the pattern of the other three. The ornament of the friezes is absent. Above all, the colour is interpretation, not measurement. Roman marble fronts were painted, but no pigment survives at Ephesus, so the red panels, the blue and gilded mouldings, the timber doors and the gilded window lattices are taken from a published reconstruction painting, not from the excavation. The ceiling of the hall is absent too, because whether the building had two storeys or three is still disputed.
